newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Rebel chief who fought, and failed to rule Angola.
newsitem.headline: Rebel chief who fought, and failed to rule Angola.

text.p: UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi waged a 30-year campaign to rule Angola.
After failing in his bid to overthrow the government, he agreed to elections in the southern African country practically destroyed in two decades of civil war.
But he lost and refused to accept his defeat in the November 1992 elections which the United Nations certified as mostly free and fair. He went back to his bush headquarters.

Under pressure to end renewed fighting that threatened to plunge the country back into civil war, he agreed to a new ceasefire in November 1994 after year-long talks sponsored by the United Nations in the Zambian capital, Lusaka.
That accord paved the way for the formation of a united national army and power-sharing.
Savimbi agreed to let members of his former rebel movement join a unity government, but declined to accept a post for himself, choosing rather the title of leader of the largest opposition party.
Savimbi's security fears caused many delays in the peace process and he exasperated many would-be intermediaries by rejecting meetings and failing to turn up at talks.
A stocky, ebullient man known by his troops as "the president", Savimbi, 62, fought first against the Portuguese, who were the country's colonial masters for nearly 500 years.
After their departure in 1975, he waged a bush war with aid from South Africa and the United States against the Soviet- and Cuban-backed MPLA government.

The war between UNITA -- the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola -- and the ruling MPLA crippled Angola's oil-based economy, killed tens of thousands of people and left hundreds of thousands homeless.

Many commentators believed Savimbi's biggest mistake was to accept aid from black Africa's number one enemy, then white-ruled South Africa. Funding from Washington, which reached about $60 million in 1990, also fuelled controversy.
The son of a railway stationmaster, he was born in the central town of Munhango on August 3, 1934.
He studied medicine at Lisbon University and political science at the University of Lausanne.

During that time he became foreign minister of the Angolan government-in-exile and vice-president of the Zaire-based Angolan Peoples' Union (UPA), which launched the first guerrilla attacks on white farms as a prelude to the independence war.
He left in 1961 to form UNITA, which he says began as an army of "12 people with knives", but later swelled to a membership estimated at up to 30,000.
